title: The Score
part: PART ONE: TWO WAYS OF KNOWING

pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: 10% chance of rain. Nari's river says: something is coming.*

Jun opened his notebook to a fresh page. He drew a line down the middle. On the left, he wrote NARI. On the right, he wrote JUN. He underlined both names in thick blue ink.

This was necessary. In Seoul, facts were facts. If he dropped a ball on the left side of the line, it went left. If he dropped it on the right, it went right. The world did not argue back. Here, the world seemed to have opinions.

Nari sat on the porch step, her chin resting on her hands. She watched him draw the line. She did not look impressed. She looked bored, in the specific way that only farm girls who have watched ten hundred seasons can be bored.

"What is that?" she asked.

"A scoreboard," said Jun. "To see who is right. It is fair."

Nari rolled her eyes so hard it looked painful. "I’m always right."

"Then the score will be very high for you," Jun said. He picked up his pen. "First contest. Go."

Nari snorted. She leaned back on her palms, balancing her weight on the rough wood. "Fine. But you’re keeping it. If I lose, I’m taking the notebook."

"You can’t take my notebook," Jun said.

"Watch me," Nari said.

The air between them tightened, crisp and electric, like the moment before a thunderclap.
pages.image: Jun, a thin boy in round black-framed glasses, sits on a wooden porch writing in a notebook, while Nari, a sunburnt girl with a long braid, leans back on her palms on the step, watching him with a bored, challenging expression.

pages.text:
The first contest was the watermelon, a large green sphere sitting on the low table. Jun tapped it with his knuckle, listening for the hollow sound his phone’s ripeness chart said meant ready. It thumped back at him, uncertain and flat.

Nari tapped it once, a single solid thud that sounded heavy and deep, like a drum being hit inside a closet.

"Ripe," she said.

"Maybe not," Jun replied, pulling up the app to check the skin texture, which suggested the color was slightly too dark.

Halmoni sliced it open. The inside was bright red, juicy, and perfect. They each ate a slice, and the first tick went under Nari’s name.

Next was the table. It wobbled, shaking a bowl of soy sauce. 

Jun reached for his phone to find a video on leveling furniture, but Nari had already reached into her pocket and pulled out a folded scrap of cloth. She wedged it under the leg, and the table stopped shaking.

"Jun," Nari said. "You didn’t even use your hands."

"I used strategy," Jun said. "And I know which way is north."

Nari squinted at the moss on the tree. "That’s south."

Jun pointed to the moss. "It grows on the wet side. In this valley, that’s north."

Nari stared at the moss, then at Jun, then at the moss again. She grunted. The third tick went under Jun’s name.
pages.image: Nari, a strong girl in a yellow T-shirt, wedges a cloth scrap under a wobbly table leg while Jun, in glasses, points to moss on a tree trunk, both focused on the task.

pages.text:
By supper, the notebook on the low table showed Nari 3, Jun 2.

Halmoni sat cross-legged nearby, mending a straw mat with a needle and thick thread. Her small hands moved in a steady rhythm while she listened to the cousins argue about the chickens. Nari had identified the sick hen by its drooping wing; Jun had read about avian flu symptoms on a forum. Nari was right.

Jun had explained the science of boiling eggs at different temperatures. Nari had eaten hers perfectly soft, without asking a single question. Jun was right.

Halmoni stopped mending. She looked at the notebook, where the numbers stared up at her, bright and stubborn.

"Aigoo," she said softly. It was a quiet sound, the kind of sigh that gets saved up for a long time. She did not look happy, nor did she look sad. She looked like she was watching two stray cats try to share one narrow windowsill.

She turned her head slowly toward the kitchen, where Harabeoji sat drinking barley tea.

"These two," Halmoni said.

Harabeoji set down his cup. He looked at Jun, then at Nari, then at the notebook.

"They are alike," he said. His voice was dry, like old leaves scraping against stone.

"We are not," Jun said.

"We are not," Nari said.

They spoke at the exact same moment, in the same tone, with the same glare.

Harabeoji took another sip of tea. He did not look surprised.
pages.image: Halmoni, a small woman in a floral top, mends a straw mat while looking toward the kitchen, and Harabeoji, a thin man in a green cap, sips tea in the background, observing the silent tension.

pages.text:
The evening air stopped moving. Heat pressed down on the yard, heavy and thick, settling over the grass like a wet wool blanket no one had folded away. The cicadas, which had been screaming since dawn, cut out all at once. The silence was so sudden and loud that Jun’s ears popped.

Nari stood up. She walked to the edge of the yard, ignoring Jun. She looked up.

Her face was flat. Her eyes were narrowed against the darkening sky. She sniffed the air, then sniffed it again.

"Tomorrow," she said.

Jun looked at his phone. The battery was at eighty percent. The screen showed the sun icon.

"Rain," Nari said. She pointed at the west. The clouds there were not white. They were purple, swollen, and low, hanging over the hills like a bruise. "A lot."

Jun pushed his glasses up. "It’s sunny."

"It’s going to rain," Nari said. She turned her back on him. "Go inside. Bring the laundry."

Jun watched the sky. It was beautiful. It was terrifying. It was definitely not sunny.
pages.image: Nari, a sunburnt girl with a long braid, stands in a darkening yard pointing at purple, swollen clouds on the horizon, while Jun, in glasses, looks on with a worried expression.

pages.text:
Jun refreshed the weather app, then checked the local station, then the satellite view. The screen stayed stubbornly bright, refusing to change its mind.

Ten percent chance of rain. Sunny.

He thrust the phone toward Nari. She did not look at the screen. Instead, she watched the sky, where the light was bending down from the clouds in a dusty, yellow haze.

"Ten percent," she said. "That means it could happen."

"It means it probably won't," Jun insisted.

"Or it could," Nari replied.

Jun looked up. The purple bruise was spreading, and the air already smelled of wet earth, even though the ground was still dry. He opened his notebook and held his pen over the page. He wanted to write a tick under his name. He wanted to be right.

But he hesitated.

Nari watched the sky with a seriousness that made his stomach feel tight. The clouds were moving faster now.

Then a single, fat drop of rain hit the notebook. It splattered on the paper, blurring the ink of the letter N in NARI.

Jun stared at the blue smudge.
pages.image: A single raindrop hits a notebook page, blurring the ink, while Jun and Nari look up at the dark, heavy sky above them.
